sections.h2: Who bills property tax in Connecticut?
sections.html:
In Connecticut each town or city assesses and bills its own property tax. The state has 169 municipalities: 19 cities, 149 towns and one borough. They sit inside eight historical counties and nine planning regions, but the property tax is a municipal matter, so there is no county bill to look for.

That shapes a sale. The assessor in your town sets the value, the board of assessment appeals hears disputes, and the tax collector sends the bill and takes payment. Population runs from 785 in Union to 148,654 in Bridgeport, and the same statutes govern both. Staffing, payment options and office hours do not, so a call to your own town hall answers more than any statewide summary.

  • Assessor: values the property and keeps the grand list.
  • Board of assessment appeals: hears appeals filed by the February deadline.
  • Tax collector: bills, collects, sends demands and handles delinquent accounts.
  • Town clerk: records the deed and collects the conveyance tax at closing.

sections.h2: How is a Connecticut home assessed?
sections.html:
Every municipality uses an October 1 assessment date and assesses property at 70 percent of its present true and actual value. Both rules come from section 12-62a of the General Statutes.

The 70 percent figure trips up many owners. A house a buyer would pay $300,000 for carries an assessed value of $210,000 on the grand list. The tax bill is then built from that assessed figure, so comparing your assessment to an asking price without adjusting for the 70 percent will make the number look too low.

The October 1 date also matters for timing. The value on that date is the one used for the bill, even if you sell the next spring. A buyer who later pays the bill is working from the status of the house as of that October, not the day of closing.

sections.h2: How often does Connecticut revalue property?
sections.html:
Towns must revalue on a five-year cycle. Under section 12-62, after October 1, 2023 each town revalues not later than the October 1 that falls five years after an assessment date set by a schedule the Secretary of the Office of Policy and Management prescribes for each revaluation zone.

In practice, your town has a revaluation year on a published schedule, and in between the assessor works from the same values with changes for new construction, demolition and corrections. Revaluation years are when assessments jump or fall for whole neighborhoods at once. If you plan to list or sell to an investor the year after a revaluation, expect the new value to show up on the next bill, and expect a buyer to ask for it.

Which year applies to your address is not something a state page can tell you. The assessor's office can say when the last revaluation took effect and when the next one is due.

sections.h2: When is the deadline to appeal a Connecticut assessment?
sections.html:
An appeal to the board of assessment appeals must be filed in writing or by electronic mail on or before February 20, according to section 12-111. The appeal has to include the owner's name, a description of the property, the reason for the appeal, the owner's own estimate of value and a signature.

The statute also gives some detail that sellers and heirs miss:

  • A person to whom title has been transferred since the assessment date can file the appeal.
  • A lessee bound by a recorded lease to pay property taxes can file.
  • The board must send hearing notice no later than March 1, and at least seven calendar days before the hearing.
  • For commercial, industrial, utility or apartment property assessed over $1,000,000, the board may decline to hold a hearing and must say so by March 1.

The deadline is strict. If you inherit a house in January and the notice sits in a drawer, February 20 does not move. Ask the assessor for the form early.

sections.h2: Can I take an assessment dispute to court?
sections.html:
Yes. Under section 12-117a, a person who is aggrieved by the board's action can apply to the superior court for the judicial district not later than two months after the date the board mailed notice of its action. The application carries a citation to the town, and it is served like a summons in a civil action.

The same section lets an appellant whose appeal the board chose not to hear go directly to the superior court. For a typical single-family house, that path is rarely needed. For a seller, the practical point is the clock: two months from the mailing date, not from the date you read the letter.

Before spending money on a court case, compare the likely tax savings with the cost and with how soon you plan to sell. A house that will close in six months often does not justify a multi-year dispute, though the right to appeal can pass to the buyer in some cases. A local attorney can look at the numbers.

sections.h2: When are Connecticut property taxes due, and what happens if I pay late?
sections.html:
Each municipality decides. Section 12-142 lets the town's legislative body choose a single payment, two semiannual installments or four quarterly installments, with the last installment due no later than 45 days before the end of the fiscal year. Your town's bill states the exact dates.

Late payments cost real money. Under section 12-146, a delinquent tax bears interest at 18 percent per year, with a minimum charge of $2 per installment unless the town votes not to impose that minimum. An installment becomes delinquent after the first day of the month following the month it was due.

StepWhat the statute says
Payment scheduleOne, two or four installments, set by the town (12-142)
Interest on late tax18 percent per year, $2 minimum per installment (12-146)
Written demandCollector sends a demand if tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date (12-155)
Levy and saleCollector prepares notices and may sell the real estate (12-157)

sections.h2: What happens at a Connecticut closing when tax is still due?
sections.html:
The unpaid bill is paid from the sale proceeds, and the buyer or title company normally confirms the balance with the tax collector before the deed is recorded. Ask the collector for a current figure with interest, because a number from last month will be short.

A seller who is behind has two realistic choices. One is a sale with the arrears cleared at the table. The other is waiting, which adds interest and, in time, a demand and a levy. Demand comes first: under section 12-155 the collector sends it when a tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date. A levy and a tax sale follow if the account stays open, as the page on Connecticut tax sales explains.

An as-is cash buyer can close around these problems, because the payoff is a line item and not a financing contingency. The offer will account for the arrears; it will not ignore them.

sections.h2: What conveyance tax applies when I sell?
sections.html:
Connecticut charges a conveyance tax on a deed when the consideration is $2,000 or more. Under section 12-494, the basic state rate is three-quarters of one percent of the price, plus one-quarter of one percent that goes to the municipality.

The state rate rises for expensive homes and for non-residential property.

  • Residential, up to $800,000: 0.75 percent state rate.
  • Residential, $800,000 to $2,500,000: 1.25 percent on the part above $800,000.
  • Residential, above $2,500,000: 2.25 percent on the part above $2,500,000.
  • Property used for something other than residential use, except unimproved land: 1.25 percent.

A $400,000 house therefore owes about $3,000 at the state rate and $1,000 at the municipal rate, or $4,000 in all. Whether the buyer or seller pays is a matter of the contract and local custom, so read the purchase agreement.

sections.h2: Which transfers are exempt from the conveyance tax?
sections.html:
Section 12-498 lists many exemptions, and a few matter for ordinary owners. Deeds between spouses are exempt, tax deeds are exempt, and so are deeds securing a debt or releasing security for one. Deeds made under certain court decrees, and deeds in lieu of foreclosure that transfer the transferor's principal residence, are listed as well.

Also exempt are transfers that only change the form of ownership with no change in beneficial ownership. A sale to an investor does not fit these categories, and a seller should assume the tax applies unless the town clerk or an attorney says otherwise.

sections.h2: What should a seller do first?
sections.html:
Pull the current bill and the assessor's record for the property, then call the tax collector for a payoff figure. Next, check whether the February 20 appeal window is still open, and whether the town is in a revaluation year.

Keep copies of every notice. If a demand or a notice of levy arrives, treat the date on it as a real deadline, because the redemption period after a tax sale is short.

faqs.q: What percent of value does Connecticut assess for property tax?
faqs.a: Seventy percent. Section 12-62a requires municipalities to assess all property at 70 percent of present true and actual value as of October 1.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal my Connecticut property assessment?
faqs.a: February 20. The appeal goes to your town's board of assessment appeals in writing or by email, and it must state the reason and your estimate of value.

faqs.q: Can I appeal to court after the board rules?
faqs.a: Yes, within two months of the date the board mailed notice of its action, by applying to the superior court for the judicial district where the town sits.

faqs.q: What interest do I owe on late Connecticut property tax?
faqs.a: Eighteen percent per year, with a $2 minimum per installment unless the town has voted not to impose that minimum.

faqs.q: Does the county bill my property tax?
faqs.a: No. The town or city assesses, bills and collects. Connecticut has eight historical counties, but the tax is assessed and collected locally.

faqs.q: What is the conveyance tax on a $400,000 Connecticut house?
faqs.a: About $4,000 at the base rates: 0.75 percent to the state and 0.25 percent to the municipality. Higher-priced homes and non-residential property pay more.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house with property tax unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance, with interest, is normally paid from the proceeds at closing. Ask the collector for a payoff figure dated near the closing.
